title: Kannappa and the living temple
hook: a hunter and a priest care for the same god, and the god bleeds
carry: after prana pratishtha, the god lives there
tomorrow: do you have to give up enjoying life to be free?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramakrishna's cup: in tantra, the offering makes the rite, not the substance. Today, a hunter who took that further than anyone.

In the hills of Kalahasti, a young hunter named Thinnan finds a Shiva linga alone in the forest, and falls in love. He has no training. So he does what he can. He carries water in his own mouth to bathe it, wears flowers in his hair to offer it, and brings it meat he's tasted first, to be sure it's good. Every morning the temple priest arrives, finds the shrine a mess, cleans it and does the proper rites, in order. Every evening the hunter comes back. Who's doing it right?
screen: `A HUNTER, A LINGA, NO TRAINING.` → `WATER, FLOWERS, TASTED MEAT.` → `THE PRIEST CLEANS UP. WHO'S RIGHT?`

segments.voice: The Periya Puranam, the Tamil lives of the Shaiva saints, tells how Shiva answered. He told the priest to hide and watch. Then blood began to flow from one eye of the linga. The hunter cut out his own eye and set it there, and the bleeding stopped. When the other eye bled, he put his foot on the spot to find it, and reached for his second eye. Shiva stopped his hand. From then on he's called Kannappa, for the eye he gave. Notice what both men believed: that the god in that stone was alive enough to thirst, and to bleed. That's the teaching behind every Hindu temple. When an image is installed, a rite called prana pratishtha, establishing the breath, invites the deity to live in it. From then on the god is a living presence, cared for like an honored guest. Texts called the Agamas, in tantra's own family, order that care: in many temples, a bell before sunrise, then waking, bathing, dressing, food, lamps, and rest at night. The priest kept the order; Kannappa had the love the order exists for, and in the story Shiva honors both. That's why temples keep their hours, morning after morning: someone is there.
screen: `THE LINGA BLEEDS.` · `KANNAPPA GIVES HIS EYE.` · `PRANA PRATISHTHA: THE BREATH IN.` · `THE AGAMAS ORDER THE CARE.` · then, large: `SOMEONE IS THERE.`

segments.voice: In many homes the morning shrine begins like a temple's: a bell or a lamp, a little water, a flower. If you pray, offer one small thing today, as to someone truly there. If you don't, bring to mind one person you look after, and walk through tomorrow's steps for them, one per breath, as for an honored guest.
What tantra actually is: here, the Agamas and prana pratishtha: a god invited to live in a temple, and cared for every day.
Pocket this: after prana pratishtha, the god lives there. Kannappa never doubted someone was there. Day sixteen-fifteen.

sources.ref: Periya Puranam (Sekkizhar), the life of Kannappa Nayanar (the hunter Thinnan at Kalahasti; water carried in his mouth, flowers in his hair, tasted meat; the temple priest's daily rites; the bleeding eye of the linga; Kannappa gives his eye)

notes: Confirm that the Agamas are fairly called 'of the same family' as the Tantras (both are tantric scripture in the broad sense), and the division: Shaiva Agamas for Shiva temples, Pancharatra or Vaikhanasa for Vishnu temples.
'Prana pratishtha, establishing the breath' is the standard dictionary sense of the rite's name, not a derivation argument; confirm.
The hook's daily cycle is a general description; individual temples differ in the number and names of rites.
